newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS - Ringgit slips as trade fears linger.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS - Ringgit slips as trade fears linger.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit weakened against the U.S. and Singapore dollars on Monday after the government released poor trade figures last week, dealers said.
"There was a big deficit after the previous month's surplus so the market is not very confident about the Malaysian economy right now," a European bank dealer in Singapore said.
On Friday, Malaysia announced a 2.1 billion ringgit deficit for April against a surplus of 1.75 billion ringgit in March, causing dollar/ringgit to spike up.
The dealer said dollar/ringgit should now be supported around 2.5140 while 2.5180/90 would provide a temporary cap.
Demand for the ringgit was also dampened after Bank Negara failed to announce any policy changes at its meeting with bankers on Friday, dealers said.
Offshore players had sold dollar/ringgit aggressively on Thursday on fears the central bank would impose capital controls similar to those of Thailand.
The Singapore dollar recovered from its lows on some selling of the ringgit/Sing cross and as the U.S. dollar came off its highs against the majors.
Dealers said the Singapore dollar had fallen as Sydney players covered short positions, triggering stop-loss buying of the U.S. dollar around 1.4280/85 and then at 1.4300.
"The market was short (the U.S. dollar) and some stops got triggered so it went to a high of 1.4323. Those who were long sold it down to take profit there," the European bank dealer said.
She said the market was now fairly well balanced and the Singapore dollar looked set to remain between 1.4250 and 1.4290.
"The market still wants to sell the ringgit/Sing cross but I think it has seen a low at 0.5650. It should go up," she added.
The cross was quoted at 0.5673/78 at 0430 GMT while dollar/Sing was at 1.4270/80.
The Thai baht continued to show a firm tone in offshore markets as the central Bank of Thailand (BOT)'s capital controls, imposed one month ago, remained firmly in place.
"It's just the usual interbank selling from Hong Kong," said one Singapore-based dealer, adding that rising baht/dollar forward premiums also put some selling pressure on the dollar.

"The two-tier market is still intact. The BOT said the controls would be temporary but so far there's no news of lifting them, which makes the market even more nervous," another Singapore dealer said.
She said the market was skeptical about the BOT's plan to revamp Thailand's forex system along the lines of Singapore's.
"Singapore is a net exporter of capital while Thailand is a net importer. Plus the baht is pegged to a basket of currencies," she said.

The baht was quoted at 24.380/24.480 to the dollar at 0430 GMT in the offshore market compared with 24.580/24.680 late on Friday. It was at 25.825/25.835 in the onshore market, against the BOT's mid-rate of 25.81.
The Indonesian rupiah hovered in a narrow range as operators kept an eye on liquidity conditions.
Dealers said the market ignored news of weekend riots in East Java where a Moslem crowd burned shops, a Protestant church and a Buddhist temple.

The incident followed a number of violent attacks on government buildings in various towns on Madura island since the May 29 general election was won by the ruling Golkar party amid claims from rivals of widespread polling irregularities.

The rupiah firmed at the open on fears of tighter liquidity due to Tuesday's weekly tax payments, but dealers said there was some dollar buying on the back of better than expected liquidity conditions.
Spot rupiah was at 2,428.0/29.0 at 0430 GMT, compared with an opening of 2,427.5/28.5.
-- Syed Azman in Kuala Lumpur (603-206 2323), Mantik Kusjanto in Jakarta (6221 384-6364), Anuchit Nguyen in Bangkok (662) 652-0642 and Sonali Desai in Singapore (65-8703090)
